title: Regular expressions
summary: Find patterns in bike IDs, station names and rider comments. Match IDs in two formats, clean names, and pull out codes and topics.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes stringr

steps.explain: stringr's functions take a regular expression, a small language for describing patterns in text, wherever they take a `pattern`.

steps.title: See what a pattern matches: str_view()

runs.purpose: read the list of bikes into `bikes`
show where a pattern for a run of digits matches in three bike IDs

steps.explain:
Most characters in a pattern match themselves, as `LB` would. `[0-9]` is a character class: any one character from 0 to 9. `+` is a quantifier: one or more of what comes before it, as many as there are.

`str_view()` marks each match with `<>`: the number at the end of each ID, whatever its format. `?` (zero or one), `*` (zero or more) and `{{5}}` (exactly five) are the other quantifiers.

steps.title: Find matches: str_detect() and anchors

runs.purpose: keep the bikes whose ID starts with LB-E-, the e-bikes
runs.task: Keep the bikes whose `bike_id` starts with "LB-E-", with `str_detect()` and the anchor `^`.

runs.purpose: count the IDs in the old format: LB, then exactly five digits and nothing else
runs.task: Count the bikes by `old_format`: whether `bike_id` is LB followed by exactly five digits and nothing else, `"^LB[0-9]{5}$"`.

steps.explain:
`str_detect()` answers `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each string, so it goes straight into `filter()` or `count()`. `^` anchors a pattern to the start of the string and `$` to its end. Without `^`, `LB-E-` would also match in the middle of a longer string. {n_e} bikes have IDs starting LB-E-.

`^LB[0-9]{{5}}$` matches only an ID that is LB and five digits from start to end: the {n_old} bikes from before the IDs gained a type letter.

steps.title: Split by pattern: separate_wider_regex()

runs.code:
bikes |>
  separate_wider_regex(
    bike_id,
    patterns = c("LB-?", type = "[CE]?", "-?", number = "[0-9]+")
  )
alternatives: bikes |> separate_wider_regex(cols = bike_id, patterns = c('LB-?', type = '[CE]?', '-?', number = '[0-9]+'))
runs.purpose: split each bike ID into its type letter and its number, whichever format it is in
runs.task: Split `bike_id` with `separate_wider_regex()`, using the patterns `"LB-?"`, `type = "[CE]?"`, `"-?"` and `number = "[0-9]+"`.

steps.explain: `separate_wider_regex()` reads each string as a sequence of patterns, one after another. Named patterns become columns; unnamed ones are matched and dropped. Each `?` makes its part optional, so the same patterns read both LB-C-00001 and LB00003: an old ID's `type` is empty. Splitting by position, as in the last lesson, couldn't handle both formats.

steps.title: Tidy names: str_replace_all()

runs.code:
stations |>
  mutate(
    clean = str_replace_all(
      name,
      c("\\s+" = " ", "’" = "'", " & " = " and ", "^St\\. " = "St ")
    ),
    .keep = "used"
  ) |>
  filter(clean != name)
alternatives: stations |> mutate(clean = name |> str_replace_all('\\s+', ' ') |> str_replace_all('’', "'") |> str_replace_all(' & ', ' and ') |> str_replace_all('^St\\. ', 'St '), .keep = 'used') |> filter(clean != name)
runs.purpose: make station names consistent and show the names that change
runs.task: Add `clean` by changing `name` with `str_replace_all()` and a named vector. Replace runs of white space (`"\\s+"`) with one space, `’` with `'`, `" & "` with `" and "`, and `"^St\\. "` with `"St "`. Keep only used columns and rows where `clean` differs from `name`.

steps.explain:
`str_replace_all()` replaces every match of a pattern. Given a named vector, it makes each replacement in turn: the names are patterns and the values what replaces them. `\\s` is any white space and `\\s+` a run of it, which mends the two spaces between "Castle" and "Gate".

A `.` in a pattern matches any character, so a full stop has to be escaped as `\.`, and in an R string the backslash itself needs escaping, which makes `\\.`. `^St\\. ` changes "St. Agnes Square" but no "St" later in a name.

steps.title: Escaping, or none at all: fixed()

runs.purpose: look for station names with a full stop, the wrong way
look for station names with a full stop, matching the dot itself

steps.explain:
As a regular expression, `.` matches any character, so every one of the {n_any} names has a match. `fixed()` turns pattern-matching off: the text is matched exactly as written, and {n_dot} name has a full stop.

Use `fixed()` when you are looking for literal text full of characters that mean something in a pattern, such as `.`, `(`, `?` or `$`; it is faster, too.

steps.title: Pull out a part: groups and ignore_case

runs.code:
survey |>
  mutate(code = str_extract(comment, "code ([A-Z0-9-]+)", group = 1)) |>
  count(code, sort = TRUE)
alternatives: survey |> mutate(code = str_match(comment, 'code ([A-Z0-9-]+)')[, 2]) |> count(code, sort = TRUE)
runs.purpose: pull out the promo code that follows the word "code" in each comment, and count the codes
runs.task: Add `code` from the capitals, digits and hyphens after "code " in `comment`. Use `str_extract()`, `"code ([A-Z0-9-]+)"` and `group = 1`. Count the codes, most first.

runs.code:
survey |>
  mutate(
    code = str_extract(
      comment,
      regex("code ([a-z0-9-]+)", ignore_case = TRUE),
      group = 1
    )
  ) |>
  count(code = str_to_upper(code), sort = TRUE)
alternatives: survey |> mutate(code = str_to_upper(str_extract(comment, regex('code ([a-z0-9-]+)', ignore_case = TRUE), group = 1))) |> count(code, sort = TRUE)
runs.purpose: do the same whatever the case, and count the codes in capitals
runs.task: Do the same with the pattern wrapped in `regex(…, ignore_case = TRUE)`, and count the codes made upper case with `str_to_upper()`.

steps.explain:
Brackets make a group, and `group = 1` asks `str_extract()` for what the first group matched rather than the whole match, so "code " is left out. Matching is case-sensitive by default, so the first count finds {n_codes} codes typed in capitals. `regex(…, ignore_case = TRUE)` matches any case and finds {n_codes_any}: some riders typed codes in lower case.

`str_to_upper()` then counts welcome10 and WELCOME10 as the same code. `|` (or) offers alternatives inside a pattern, as in `"brake|saddle"`.
